questions.q: What resource does speculative decoding spend in order to reduce the number of sequential decode steps?
options: Extra GPU memory for the KV cache
Extra GPU compute, which decode's memory-bound nature normally leaves underused
Extra network bandwidth between GPUs
Extra disk storage for model checkpoints
questions.explain: Decode is memory-bound, meaning the GPU's compute units are often underused during normal decode. Speculative decoding spends that spare compute verifying multiple drafted tokens in one parallel pass.

questions.q: What roles do the draft model and target model play?
options: The draft model is the final authority; the target model only proposes tokens
The draft model quickly proposes several candidate tokens; the target model verifies all of them in a single parallel forward pass
Both models run completely independently with no verification step
The target model is always smaller and faster than the draft model
questions.explain: A small, fast draft model proposes several tokens in a row, and the large target model checks all of them at once in a parallel forward pass rather than one sequential step per token.

questions.q: Why is the verification step described as more than just 'checking for a match'?
options: Because it skips verification entirely and trusts the draft model
Because it uses a rejection-sampling procedure that guarantees the final output has exactly the same probability distribution as standard decoding
Because it always rejects every drafted token regardless of accuracy
Because it only verifies the first drafted token and ignores the rest
questions.explain: The verification procedure is a specific rejection-sampling method that preserves the target model's exact output distribution, making speculative decoding a speed optimization rather than a quality trade-off.

questions.q: What happens when a drafted token is rejected during verification?
options: The entire request is cancelled and restarted from the beginning
Everything after that token in the draft is discarded, and the target model samples that position itself before continuing
The draft model is immediately replaced with a different model
Nothing — rejected tokens are used anyway
questions.explain: On rejection, the drafted tokens after that point are discarded, and the target model re-samples the rejected position itself, after which drafting can resume from there.

questions.q: Why is acceptance rate the key metric for deciding whether speculative decoding is worthwhile?
options: Acceptance rate measures how much GPU memory the draft model uses
If acceptance rate is low, the cost of running the draft model isn't recovered, since verification still mostly falls back to one-token-at-a-time generation
Acceptance rate has no effect on whether speculative decoding helps
Acceptance rate only matters when using prompt lookup decoding
questions.explain: Speculative decoding only pays off when drafted tokens are accepted often enough to offset the cost of drafting. A low acceptance rate means most steps still fall back to standard sequential decoding.
